title: Society of Critical Care Medicine Guidelines for the Treatment of Heat Stroke
source: Society of Critical Care Medicine / Critical Care Medicine
summary: SCCM's GRADE-informed heat-stroke guideline strongly recommends active rather than passive cooling, with cold- or ice-water immersion delivering the fastest cooling when feasible. It strongly recommends against dantrolene. Both strong recommendations rely on very-low-certainty evidence; good-practice guidance discourages routine antipyretics for temperature control.
findings: Strong recommendation for active rather than passive cooling (very-low-certainty evidence).
Cold- or ice-water immersion is the fastest cooling approach when feasible.
Good-practice statement discourages routine antipyretics for heat-stroke temperature reduction.
comparator: Passive cooling and alternative measures across guideline questions; not a single trial.
population: Patients with exertional or classic heat stroke in acute and critical-care settings.
limitations: Evidence supporting both strong recommendations is very low certainty and immersion may not be feasible. Official SCCM recommendation material and PubMed abstract were reviewed, not the complete journal article.
intervention: Rapid active cooling and guideline assessment of temperature-modifying medications.
whyItMatters: Begin effective physical cooling promptly in suspected heat stroke instead of relying on antipyretics or dantrolene. Adapt cooling modality to feasibility and concurrent stabilization.
evidenceNotes: Official SCCM recommendations and primary PubMed abstract PMID 39982186 DOI 10.1097/CCM.0000000000006551 reviewed. Epub February 21, 2025; society page dated February 22, February 1 print. Complete journal guideline not reviewed. No verified correction found in targeted check.
primaryEndpoint: Guideline outcomes on cooling and clinical treatment, not a trial primary endpoint.
guidelineStrength: Strong for active cooling and against dantrolene, both based on very-low-certainty evidence; other recommendations are good-practice statements.
